analysis.one_liner: Directs the EPA to ban discharges of plastic pellets and pre-production plastic into US waterways.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 89 cosponsors, never got a committee vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Plastic pellets — the tiny raw beads melted down to make nearly every plastic product — spill by the trillions from factories, trucks, and rail cars into rivers, lakes, and oceans, where they soak up toxins and enter the food chain. This bill would have required the EPA to write a rule within 60 days banning those discharges and writing the ban into every wastewater and stormwater permit for facilities that make, use, package, or transport the pellets. It was introduced in March 2024 with 89 cosponsors but never received a vote in the committee it was assigned to, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who swim, fish, and drink from the nation's waterways, and coastal communities that bear the cleanup and fisheries costs of plastic pellet pollution. Because pellets are so small, ordinary water treatment does not catch them; stopping them at the factory and shipping stage is the only practical fix. Commercial and recreational fishing industries that lose stock to plastic-contaminated waters would also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who fish, swim, and drink tap water

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA, within 60 days of enactment, to issue a final rule prohibiting the discharge of plastic pellets and other pre-production plastic into waters of the United States, including through wastewater and stormwater runoff.

Extends the ban to any point source that makes, uses, packages, or transports plastic pellets — not just the plastic production plants already covered by existing EPA effluent rules — closing a gap that lets shippers and packaging facilities discharge freely.
Writes the prohibition into all wastewater, stormwater, and other permits issued under the Clean Water Act's delegated permit programs, so states cannot simply decline to enforce it.

analysis.who_pays: Plastic polymer producers, plastic molding and forming plants, and the shipping, packaging, and transport companies that handle pellets. They would need containment systems, spill controls, and permit compliance to keep pellets out of drains and waterways — real compliance costs in a high-volume industrial supply chain, though far cheaper than the waterway cleanup the pellets currently force on others.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on manufacturers and transporters of pellets, and an absolute discharge prohibition gives facilities no allowance for accidental releases, which could mean costly enforcement even for negligible spills.

Ordering a final rule within 60 days of enactment leaves the EPA almost no time for the usual public comment and technical review that tailors limits to different facility types, raising the risk of a rule that is quickly litigated or poorly fitted to real operations.
It addresses pellets at the source but does nothing about the plastic already in waterways or the consumer plastic waste that makes up most plastic pollution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — stopping a persistent, essentially impossible-to-clean-up pollutant at its source — is large and permanent for waterways, fisheries, and drinking water. The costs are containment and permit compliance for a specific industrial supply chain, and the bill's 60-day rulemaking deadline is unusually fast and could invite legal challenges. On balance the trade favors the public, which is what makes the bill's quiet death without even a committee vote notable.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its water subcommittee the week it was introduced, and neither ever took it up; it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mike Levin introduced the bill on March 12, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where committee action ended.
The bill attracted 89 cosponsors — 88 House Democrats and 1 House Republican — but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.

The bill required the EPA to issue a final rule within 60 days of enactment banning discharges of plastic pellets and other pre-production plastic into US waters, including through wastewater and stormwater, and to write that ban into all relevant Clean Water Act permits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastic pellet producers and the companies that transport and package them are better off, since they avoided a mandatory discharge ban and the containment spending it would require. Waterways and the people who use them got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic — 88 of the 89 cosponsors — and the Republican-run committee that controlled its fate never acted on it.

industries.industry: Plastic resin and pre-production plastic manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would prohibit these facilities from discharging pellets into wastewater and stormwater, requiring containment and permit compliance. Pellet spills are the main way trillions of microplastic beads enter US waterways, so the industry's cost savings from loose handling come directly at the public's expense.

industries.industry: Plastic molding, forming, packaging, and transport companies
industries.note: The bill extends the discharge ban beyond production plants to any point source that makes, uses, packages, or transports pellets, pulling shippers and packagers into Clean Water Act permitting and spill prevention for the first time.

industries.industry: Commercial and recreational fisheries and water-dependent tourism
industries.note: Pellet pollution contaminates the waters these industries depend on; a source ban would reduce the microplastic burden in fish habitats and swimming areas.
